Submissions of the Appellant / Prudent Arc Limited
7.
Prudent ARC Limited is acting in its capacity as trustee of Prudent Trust
97/24, Prudent Trust 81/23, Prudent Trust 108/25, Prudent Trust 102/25,
Prudent Trust 114/25, Prudent Trust 114/25 SR II, Prudent Trust 114/25
SR III, and Prudent Trust 114/25 SR IV (“Appellant”), and also being the
financial creditor holding 94.86% of the voting share in the committee of
creditors (“CoC”) of Worlds Window Exim Private Limited (“Corporate Debtor”).

8.
Impugned Order is based on the erroneous premise that the CoC’s
approval of a resolution plan which proposes to pay less than the liquidation
value of the Corporate Debtor will breach the provisions of the Code. The
Impugned Order rejects the Resolution Plan primarily on the ground that the
Total Resolution Amount (INR 7,00,00,000/-) offered in the Resolution Plan
is lower than the Liquidation Value of the Corporate Debtor (INR
9,42,25,758/-). The total resolution amount offered under a resolution plan
can be less than the liquidation value of the corporate debtor, and no
provision of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (“Code”) or the
Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (Insolvency Resolution Process for

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1725 and 1706 of 2026 10 of 37

Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 (“CIRP Regulations”) requires the total
amount offered under a resolution plan to match or exceed the corporate
debtor’s liquidation value.

9.
The Appellant relied on the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in
Maharashtra Seamless Limited v. Padmanabhan Venkatesh & Ors., (2020)
11 SCC 467 [paras 28 and 30], and the same decision was further upheld in
State Bank of India v. Accord Life Spec (P) Ltd. & Ors., 2020 SCC OnLine
SC 554 [para 3], unequivocally settling the position on this issue.

10.
Without prejudice to the above, Section 30(2)(b) of the Code
protects/guarantees that the dissenting financial creditors receive at least
their entitlement under Section 53 i.e. liquidation value. The Code does not
prescribe any minimum payment to be paid to financial creditors who vote in
favour of the resolution plan. The Appellant (holding 94.86% voting share)
voted in favour of the Resolution Plan, and Punjab National Bank (“PNB”)
(holding 5.14% of the voting share) did not cast a vote and is therefore the
sole dissenting financial creditor. It is submitted that Clause 3.4(ii) of the
Resolution Plan expressly guarantees the minimum payment required to be
paid to the dissenting financial creditors in compliance with the terms of the
Section 30(2)(b) of the Code by expressly stating that “In the event any
Financial Creditor dissents, such Dissenting Financial Creditors shall be paid
the minimum amount as is required in terms of Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC.”
Therefore, as a dissenting financial creditor, PNB’s statutory entitlement
under Section 30(2)(b) of the Code is expressly protected under Clause 3.4(ii)
of the Resolution Plan, which guarantees that any dissenting financial

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1725 and 1706 of 2026 11 of 37

creditor shall be paid the minimum amount required under Section 30(2)(b)
of the Code.

11.
Without prejudice to the above, it is also submitted that the Ld. NCLT’s
own comparison between the Total Resolution Amount and Liquidation Value
was incomplete and unsustainable as the Ld. NCLT failed to take into account
the import of Clause 3.7(b) of the Resolution Plan, which entitles the CoC to
the Corporate Debtor’s cash, cash equivalents and other realisable financial
assets, valued at approximately INR 1,15,66,063/-, taking the aggregate
recovery available to Financial Creditors to approximately INR 8,15,66,063/.

12.
The decision of the CoC to approve or reject the resolution plan and the
value proposed therein falls squarely within the commercial wisdom of the
CoC, which has consistently been held to be non-justiciable. Reliance is
placed on K. Sashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank & Ors., (2019) 12 SCC
150 [paragraph 52-55]; Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Ltd.
v. Satish Kumar Gupta & Ors., (2020) 8 SCC 531 [paras 64 and 73].

13.
In view of the foregoing, the rejection of the Resolution Plan solely on
the ground that the Total Resolution Amount is lower than the Liquidation
Value of the Corporate Debtor is contrary to settled law and unsustainable.
The Resolution Plan was approved by the CoC with 94.86% voting share in
exercise of the CoC’s commercial wisdom which is not amenable to judicial
review by the Ld. NCLT. The Impugned Order is therefore liable to be set aside
on this ground.

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1725 and 1706 of 2026 12 of 37

14.
The Impugned Order proceeds on the erroneous premise that the
Resolution Plan does not sufficiently address the cause of default. The Ld.
NCLT erred in holding that the Resolution Plan violated Regulation 38(3)(a)
merely because Clause 2.14 states that the Resolution Applicant is not “fully
aware” of the cause of default. It is submitted that Clause 2.14 identifies, from
the financial statements annexed to the Information Memorandum, that the
Corporate Debtor had sustained losses, no turnover, and liabilities exceeding
assets, and proposes measures to address these issues. Regulation 38(3)(a)
only requires the plan to address the cause of default, which as per plain
reading of the terms of the Resolution Plan including Clause 2.14, duly does.

15.
Further, the adequacy of how a resolution plan addresses the cause of
default falls within the commercial wisdom of the CoC and is not open to re-
appraisal by the Ld. NCLT absent a violation of Section 30(2). By reassessing
the adequacy of Clause 2.14 instead of confining itself to Section 30(2), the
Ld. NCLT impermissibly substituted its own view for that of the CoC. The
scope of jurisdiction of the Ld. NCLT and scrutiny and intervention of the Ld.
NCLT under Section 31 is clearly settled in Arun Kumar Jagatramka v.
Jindal Steel & Power Ltd., (2021) 7 SCC 474 [para 95]; Vashishth Builders
and Engineers Ltd. v. Trishul Dream Homes Ltd., Company Appeal
(AT)(Insolvency) No. 732 of 2025 [paras 28-29].

16.
The Ld. NCLT exceeded its jurisdiction by limiting the Appellant’s
entitlement as an assignee, having itself recorded the assignment of debt in
favour of the Appellant. The Impugned Order, at paragraph 11, unlawfully
directs that the Appellant “.... It is made clear that the ARC will not get the

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1725 and 1706 of 2026 13 of 37

share from distributable amount in excess of the amount what it has paid to
Central Bank of India and the excess amount if becomes payable to assignee
of the debt of Central Bank of India would be paid to the assigner viz. Central
Bank of India....” It is humbly submitted that the Ld. NCLT exceeded its
jurisdiction in holding the above, and the above direction is contrary to settled
law. The assignment of the debt from Central Bank of India to Prudent Trust
114/25 SR IV was carried out in accordance with Securitisation and
Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act,
2002 (“SARFAESI Act”) and constituted a true sale of the financial debt in
favour of Prudent Trust 114/25 SR IV. The assignment was intimated to the
Ld. NCLT vide I.A. No. 5916 of 2025 in accordance with Regulation 28 of the
CIRP Regulations. Further, the I.A. No. 5916 of 2025 was allowed by the Ld.
NCLT vide its order dated January 29, 2026 expressly taking the assignment
on record. The above assignment constitutes a valid contractual right of the
Appellant as an assignee, vesting it with the full rights of a financial creditor
under Section 5(7) of the Code, including the right to receive distributions in
proportion to its admitted claim for the debt assigned to it, and not limited to
the consideration paid for acquiring the debt. Having itself accepted and taken
the assignment on record, and having recognised the Appellant as the
financial creditor in place of the assignor banks by its own order dated
January 29, 2026, the Ld. NCLT could not have revisited or qualified the
consequences of that very assignment by capping the Appellant’s entitlement.
Such a direction is not only entirely contrary to law and the Appellant’s
contractual rights, but also tantamount to a revision of the Ld. NCLT’s own
earlier order accepting the assignment for which the Ld. NCLT does not have

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1725 and 1706 of 2026 14 of 37

jurisdiction. In light of the above, it is submitted that the aforementioned
direction in the Impugned Order is completely impermissible and shall be
expunged as unwarranted and prejudicial. In any event, such direction is
beyond the scope of the Ld. NCLT’s jurisdiction under Section 31 of the Code,
which is confined to examining whether the Resolution Plan meets the
requirements of Section 30(2) of the Code.

17.
Valuation of the assets of the Corporate Debtor does not arise for
consideration in the present appeal. The Valuation Corporate Debtor’s assets
was never challenged by any party before the Ld. NCLT, nor does the
Impugned Order record any adverse finding on valuation. On the contrary,
the Ld. NCLT expressly observed that it could not interfere with the valuation
of the Corporate Debtor’s assets or reject the Resolution Plan merely because
the Total Resolution Amount was lower than the Liquidation Value. In these
circumstances, there is no question on validity or veracity of the valuation in
the present appeal.

18.
Ld. NCLT erred in law by ordering liquidation of the Corporate Debtor
without first following the procedure set out in the proviso inserted to Section
31(2) of the Code. Without prejudice to the foregoing, it is submitted that even
if the Resolution Plan suffered from the deficiencies identified in the Impugned
Order, the Ld. NCLT could not have directly proceeded to reject the Resolution
Plan and order liquidation of the Corporate Debtor. As on the date of the
Impugned Order, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act,
2026 (“2026 Amendment Act”) was in force, and required the Ld. NCLT: (i)
under the proviso to Section 31(2) of the Code, to first afford the CoC an

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1725 and 1706 of 2026 15 of 37

opportunity to cure any defects in the Resolution Plan before rejecting it; and
(ii) under Section 33(1A) of the Code, before directing liquidation, to consider
restoration of the CIRP for a fresh invitation of resolution plans.

19.
It is well settled that liquidation is a measure of last resort [see Duncans
Industries Limited v. A.J. Agrochem, (2019) 9 SCC 725, para 7.4]. In the
present case, the CIRP had yielded a Resolution Plan approved by the CoC
with 94.86% voting share. Any perceived deficiencies were confined to the
Plan and did not justify bypassing the statutory requirement of providing
opportunity to cure the defects in the Resolution Plan or considering
restoration of the CIRP, before directing liquidation.

20.
The Impugned Order is therefore liable to be set aside on this ground
alone, as the mandatory procedure prescribed under the amended provisions
of the Code was not followed.
Submissions of Respondent No. 1 / Mr. Manish Agarwal, Resolution
Professional

21.
The present Appeal is preferred by Prudent Arc Limited (as trustee of
the Prudent Trusts), a Financial Creditor holding 94.86% of the voting share
in the Committee of Creditors (“CoC”) of Worlds Window Exim Private Limited
(“Corporate Debtor”), against order dated 14.08.2026 passed by Hon’ble NCLT
(“NCLT”) in I.A. No. 32 of 2026 in C.P. (IB) No. 108 of 2025 (“Impugned Order”)
rejecting the resolution plan (“Plan”) of Respondent No. 2 (“SRA”), approved
by the CoC, in its 9th CoC meeting held on 23.04.2026, with 94.86% voting
share.

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1725 and 1706 of 2026 16 of 37

22.
Ld. NCLT rejected the Plan as being violative of (i) Section 30(2)(b) of the
Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (“Code”), the Plan value (INR
7,00,00,000/-) being less than the liquidation value (INR 9,42,25,758/-) and
(ii) Regulation 38(3)(a) of the IBBI (Resolution Process for Corporate Persons)
Regulations, 2016 (“CIRP Regulations”), the SRA being unaware of the cause
of default, and initiated liquidation under Section 33(1)(b) of the Code.

23.
The Corporate Debtor, an asset holding company with no operations, is
Corporate Guarantor of Magnifico Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (Principal Borrower), who
was admitted into CIRP on 07.08.2024 and its plan was approved by NCLT
on 11.06.2026. The findings of the NCLT in the Impugned Order and the
grounds raised by Respondent No. 1 against each are set out below:
"NCLT observed it “may not interfere with valuation of
assets of CD nor can it nix the Resolution Plan on the
ground that the plan value is less than the liquidation
value”.

24.
No breach of section 30(2) of the Code: Despite NCLT’s observation at
paragraph 6, the NCLT rejected the Plan on that very ground, assuming that

CoC. The CoC then approved a Plan offering INR 7,00,00,000/-, which is less
than the liquidation value, and the counsel for the suspended promoters
accepted it at once. We have held that a plan value below the liquidation value
is not illegal by itself. But it is a relevant fact when it is seen along with these
other facts. These facts, together with the failure to meet Regulation 38(3)(a),
justify the doubt of the Adjudicating Authority about the Plan. We do not rest
our decision on suspicion alone.

58.
The adjudicating authority has also ordered an investigation into the
affairs of the corporate debtor under Sections 43, 45, 50, and 66 of the Code
and observed as follows:
“The liquidator would investigate the affairs of the CD and would take all
legal steps including filing and pursuing applications under Sections 43, 45,

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1725 and 1706 of 2026 34 of 37

50 and 66 of the Code to disgorge the properties and assets of the CD for
being utilized to discharge its debt.”

59.
Once the Adjudicating Authority found suspicion about the affairs of
the Corporate Debtor, in a case where an asset holding company had availed
a big loan and the assignment was made while the insolvency was going on,
it was proper to order an independent investigation. The direction is limited
to an inquiry by the Liquidator and to such applications as he may file under
Sections 43, 45, 50 and 66 of the Code. The persons concerned will be heard
in those proceedings before any order is passed against them. We find no
infirmity in this direction.
E. Direction limiting the entitlement of the assignee
60.
The Appellant has questioned the direction in para 11 of the Impugned
Order, which reads as follows:
“11.
.... It is made clear that the ARC will not get the share from
distributable amount in excess of the amount what it has paid to Central
Bank of India and the excess amount if becomes payable to assignee of the
debt of Central Bank of India would be paid to the assigner viz. Central
Bank of India....”

61.
The Appellant says that the Adjudicating Authority had taken the
assignment on record and so could not limit its entitlement. The direction was
given on the footing that the assignment was open to suspicion. But the affairs
of the Corporate Debtor, including the assignment, are yet to be investigated.
What an assignee is entitled to receive will depend on the outcome of that
investigation and on the facts and the law applicable. We think that the
direction is premature and should wait until the investigation is over. We
therefore set aside the direction in para 11 of the Impugned Order. All rights

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1725 and 1706 of 2026 35 of 37

and contentions of the parties on this question are kept open, to be decided
by the Adjudicating Authority at the proper stage.
F. Proviso to Section 31(2) and Section 33(1A) of the Code
62.
The Appellant and the Resolution Professional contend that, even if the
Plan was defective, the Adjudicating Authority could not reject it and order
liquidation directly. They rely on the proviso inserted in Section 31(2) by the
2026 Amendment Act, which deals with giving notice to the CoC to rectify
defects before a plan is rejected, and on Section 33(1A), which deals with
restoration of the CIRP before liquidation is ordered. For this purpose, we take
it that these provisions were in force on the date of the Impugned Order.

63.
These provisions are enabling in nature. The proviso to Section 31(2)
allows the Adjudicating Authority to give notice to the CoC to rectify defects
before it rejects a plan. Section 33(1A) allows it to consider restoration of the
CIRP before it directs liquidation. Neither provision makes it compulsory for
the Adjudicating Authority to follow that course in every case. It may do so
when it is satisfied that the facts call for it. Here, the Adjudicating Authority
has decided on liquidation. We have gone through the facts and the material
on record. The defects in this Plan are not minor drafting gaps. They relate to
a mandatory content of the Plan and to doubts about the conduct of the
process, which are now to be investigated. A notice to rectify, or a restoration
of the CIRP, would not meet these concerns. We also do not find it necessary
to adopt any course other than liquidation.

64.
The Appellant and the Resolution Professional rely on the principle that
liquidation is the last resort. In Duncans Industries Ltd. v. A.J. Agrochem
(supra) (para 7.4), the Supreme Court said:

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1725 and 1706 of 2026 36 of 37

“The winding up/liquidation of the company shall be the last resort and
only on an eventuality when the corporate insolvency resolution process
fails.”

65.
In Essar Steel (supra) (paras 71 and 72), quoting Swiss Ribbons, the
Supreme Court also observed that the Preamble does not refer to liquidation,
“which is only availed of as a last resort if there is either no resolution plan or
the resolution plans submitted are not up to the mark”. We accept this
principle. But the stage for the last resort has come in this case. The CIRP
has not produced a plan that meets the requirements of Section 30(2), and
the only Plan before the Adjudicating Authority was not up to the mark.
Liquidation was therefore the course left under the Code.
Conclusions
66.
Our conclusions are as follows:
(i)
The Plan does not demonstrate that it addresses the cause of default,
and so it violates Regulation 38(3)(a) of the CIRP Regulations. It therefore does
not meet Section 30(2)(f) of the Code. This is a check within Section 31(1) and
not a matter of the commercial wisdom of the CoC.
(ii)
The finding that the dissenting financial creditor would receive less than
its entitlement under Section 30(2)(b) is not sustained, as Clause 3.4 of the
Plan protects its entitlement and no provision requires a plan to match the
liquidation value. This does not change the result of the appeals.

(iii)
The overall circumstances of the case support the doubt of the
Adjudicating Authority about the Plan. The direction for investigation by the
Liquidator, including applications under Sections 43, 45, 50 and 66 of the
Code, is upheld.

Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1725 and 1706 of 2026 37 of 37

(iv)
The direction in para 11 of the Impugned Order, limiting the share of
the assignee, is premature and is set aside. All contentions on this question
are kept open.

(v)
The proviso to Section 31(2) and Section 33(1A) of the Code are not
mandatory in every case. The Adjudicating Authority was justified in rejecting
the Plan and in ordering liquidation of the Corporate Debtor under Section
33(1)(b) of the Code.
Order
67.
For the reasons stated above, we do not find any infirmity in the
Impugned Order dated 14.08.2026, except for the direction in para 11 limiting
the entitlement of the assignee, which is set aside as stated above. Company
Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1725 of 2026 and Company Appeal (AT)
(Insolvency) No. 1706 of 2026 are accordingly dismissed. The order of the
Adjudicating Authority rejecting the Resolution Plan, directing liquidation of
the Corporate Debtor and directing investigation into its affairs stands
upheld, subject to the modification made above. No order as to costs. Pending
applications, if any, are closed.

any other part of the Plan that states the cause of default or how it will be
addressed.

We therefore hold that the Plan does not satisfy Regulation 38(3)(a) and
so does not meet the requirement of Section 30(2)(f) of the Code. The
Adjudicating Authority was right in holding that the Plan could not be
approved on this ground. This ground is enough by itself to justify the
rejection of the Plan.
C. Plan value and Section 30(2)(b) of the Code
51.
The Adjudicating Authority also held that the Plan violates Section
30(2)(b). Its findings are as follows:
“6.
It is borne out of the record that one of the Financial Creditor viz.
Punjab National Bank did not vote in favour of the plan, thus it emerges as
dissenting creditor. It may be so that this Tribunal may not interfere with
valuation of assets of CD nor can it nix the Resolution Plan on the ground
that the plan value is less than liquidation value, but once the plan value is
less than liquidation value, the share offered to dissenting secured
Financial Creditor would be less than the amount to be paid to it in the
event of liquidation of the CD under Section 53 of the Code. During the
course of hearing, Mr. Abhishek, the Ld. Counsel for the RP tried to espouse
that when Rs. 7 Cr. would be distributed amongst the secured Financial
Creditors it may be so that the PNB will get the same amount which could
be given to it in the event of liquidation of the CD under Section 53 of the
Code. In such situation, the amount payable to other secured creditor
would be in violation of explanation 1 to sub-section 2 of Section 30 of the
Code. It is no longer res integra that the explanation had be read as part of
the statute...

52.
The Adjudicating Authority first said that it cannot reject a plan merely
because the plan value is below the liquidation value. It then held that, since
the plan value is below the liquidation value, the dissenting creditor would
get less than its entitlement. This assumption does not take into account the
terms of the Plan. Punjab National Bank is the only dissenting financial
creditor. Clause 3.4(ii) of the Plan provides: “In the event any Financial
Creditor dissents, such Dissenting Financial Creditors shall be paid the
minimum amount as is required in terms of Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC.” The
Resolution Professional has also pointed to Clause 3.4(iii), under which the
dissenting creditor is paid in cash and in priority to the assenting creditors.
The Plan thus guarantees the entitlement of the dissenting creditor under
Section 30(2)(b).

53.
Section 30(2)(b) protects the dissenting financial creditors by ensuring
that they receive at least their entitlement under Section 53, that is, the
liquidation value. The Code does not fix any minimum payment for the
financial creditors who vote for the plan. On the lower plan value, the
Supreme Court said in Maharashtra Seamless (supra) (para 28):
“No provision in the Code or Regulations has been brought to our notice
under which the bid of any resolution applicant has to match liquidation
value arrived at in the manner provided in Regulation 35 of the Insolvency
and Bankruptcy Board of India (Insolvency Resolution Process for
Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016.”

has categorically held as under:
"No provision in the Code or Regulations has been brought to our notice
under which the bid of any resolution applicant has to match liquidation

and Bankruptcy Board of India (Insolvency Resolution Process for

The amount offered under a plan and its distribution among the creditors are
matters for the commercial wisdom of the CoC, as held in Essar Steel and K.
Sashidhar (para 52), which has been extracted below:
“52.
As aforesaid, upon receipt of a “rejected” resolution plan the
adjudicating authority (NCLT) is not expected to do anything more; but is
obligated to initiate liquidation process under Section 33(1) of the I&B Code.
The legislature has not endowed the adjudicating authority (NCLT) with the
jurisdiction or authority to analyse or evaluate the commercial decision of CoC
much less to enquire into the justness of the rejection of the resolution plan
by the dissenting financial creditors. From the legislative history and the
background in which the I&B Code has been enacted, it is noticed that a
completely new approach has been adopted for speeding up the recovery of
the debt due from the defaulting companies. In the new approach, there is a
calm period followed by a swift resolution process to be completed within 270
days (outer limit) failing which, initiation of liquidation process has been made
inevitable and mandatory. In the earlier regime, the corporate debtor could

is an intrinsic assumption that financial creditors are fully informed about the
viability of the corporate debtor and feasibility of the proposed resolution

resolution plan and assessment made by their team of experts. The opinion on

A plan value lower than the liquidation value is therefore not, by itself, a
ground to hold that a plan violates Section 30(2)(b).

We agree with the Appellant on this point. The finding that the

sustained, in view of Clause 3.4 of the Plan. The further remark of the
Adjudicating Authority on Explanation 1 to Section 30(2) was made in the
same context, and we do not need to decide it. This does not, however, help
the Appellant. The Adjudicating Authority did not reject the Plan on this

F. Proviso to Section 31(2) and Section 33(1A) of the Code
62.
The Appellant and the Resolution Professional contend that, even if the
Plan was defective, the Adjudicating Authority could not reject it and order
liquidation directly. They rely on the proviso inserted in Section 31(2) by the
2026 Amendment Act, which deals with giving notice to the CoC to rectify
defects before a plan is rejected, and on Section 33(1A), which deals with
restoration of the CIRP before liquidation is ordered. For this purpose, we take
it that these provisions were in force on the date of the Impugned Order.

63.
These provisions are enabling in nature. The proviso to Section 31(2)
allows the Adjudicating Authority to give notice to the CoC to rectify defects
before it rejects a plan. Section 33(1A) allows it to consider restoration of the
CIRP before it directs liquidation. Neither provision makes it compulsory for
the Adjudicating Authority to follow that course in every case. It may do so
when it is satisfied that the facts call for it. Here, the Adjudicating Authority
has decided on liquidation. We have gone through the facts and the material
on record. The defects in this Plan are not minor drafting gaps. They relate to
a mandatory content of the Plan and to doubts about the conduct of the
process, which are now to be investigated. A notice to rectify, or a restoration
of the CIRP, would not meet these concerns. We also do not find it necessary
to adopt any course other than liquidation.

64.

liquidation is the last resort. In Duncans Industries Ltd. v. A.J. Agrochem
(supra) (para 7.4), the Supreme Court said:

Supreme Court also observed that the Preamble does not refer to liquidation,
“which is only availed of as a last resort if there is either no resolution plan or
the resolution plans submitted are not up to the mark”. We accept this
principle. But the stage for the last resort has come in this case. The CIRP
has not produced a plan that meets the requirements of Section 30(2), and
the only Plan before the Adjudicating Authority was not up to the mark.
Liquidation was therefore the course left under the Code.
Conclusions
66.
Our conclusions are as follows:
(i)
The Plan does not demonstrate that it addresses the cause of default,
and so it violates Regulation 38(3)(a) of the CIRP Regulations. It therefore does
not meet Section 30(2)(f) of the Code. This is a check within Section 31(1) and
not a matter of the commercial wisdom of the CoC.
(ii)
The finding that the dissenting financial creditor would receive less than
its entitlement under Section 30(2)(b) is not sustained, as Clause 3.4 of the
Plan protects its entitlement and no provision requires a plan to match the
liquidation value. This does not change the result of the appeals.

(iii)
The overall circumstances of the case support the doubt of the
Adjudicating Authority about the Plan. The direction for investigation by the
Liquidator, including applications under Sections 43, 45, 50 and 66 of the
Code, is upheld.
